### Chapter 13 — The lessons pipeline

_Permalink: https://holonograph.ai/guide/lessons-pipeline_

Chapter 13

# The lessons pipeline

        A system's interactions contain the information that should make it better. This chapter is how Holonograph turns that information into shipped improvements: captured human overrides cluster, the drafter proposes concrete corrective artifacts for each cluster, a named human approves or rejects at the gate, and only then does anything get published. Nothing bypasses the gate.

## What it is

        A five-step pipeline, one endpoint per step:

          - **Override**: a human corrects the system's output. Recorded as first-class ground truth: *what the system produced* next to *what good looks like*.

          - **Cluster**: similar overrides group together, so one fix can address a pattern instead of a single instance.

          - **Draft**: the drafter proposes a concrete corrective artifact for a cluster. Four kinds: `skill`, `lesson`, `fixture`, `code-change-recommendation`.

          - **Approve or reject**: a named approver reads the draft, edits or rejects. This is the gate.

          - **Publish**: an approved draft becomes substrate. Versioned, captured, and attributable in future readings like any other change.

## Why it matters

        Feedback in most agentic systems is either noted-and-forgotten or wired into a slow fine-tuning loop. Neither is a good fit for the operator running a real product on a real timeline. The lessons pipeline gives that operator a third path: *capture the correction, cluster the pattern, ship a concrete artifact through a named gate*. The artifact (a new skill, a lesson, a fixture, a code change) is the smallest unit of "the system got better," and every one of them is attributable in future drift readings.

          The gate is the point
          Nothing published in this pipeline ships without a named approver on record. A rejected draft leaves an audit trail; an approved one does too. The gate is what makes this pipeline safe to run against production behavior.

## How to use it

### 1. Record an override

        When a human corrects the system, capture both sides:

```
POST /hil/override
x-holonograph-run-mode: production
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "agentId": "billing-triage",
  "surfaceId": "classify-intent",
  "correlationId": "corr_01H...",
  "originalOutput": { /* what the system produced */ },
  "correctedOutput": { /* what the human sent instead */ },
  "rationale": "Refund lookup wasn't invoked; agent guessed.",
  "tags": ["fix_tier=tool-input-schema"]
}
```

        Response: an `eventId`. The override is now in the substrate, tagged and correlated with the original call.

### 2. Cluster overrides over a window

        Run the clustering endpoint to group similar overrides, usually on a schedule (nightly), sometimes on-demand when an operator wants to see what's been building up.

```
POST /lessons/cluster
x-holonograph-run-mode: production
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "surfaceId": "classify-intent",
  "since": "2026-07-01T00:00:00Z",
  "until": "2026-07-05T00:00:00Z"
}
```

        Response: `clusters[]` plus a total `eventCount`. Each cluster carries its member override ids and a summary shape the drafter can consume.

### 3. Draft a corrective artifact

        Ask the drafter to propose an artifact for a cluster. Pick the kind that fits:

Kind	When it fits

`skill`	The agent needs a new capability it doesn't currently have.

`lesson`	The agent has the capability but keeps using it wrong. A prompt-level correction is enough.

`fixture`	The correction should be a reproducible check, so future regressions get caught before shipping.

`code-change-recommendation`	The problem lives in code (tool schema, dispatch logic) and needs a developer to fix.

```
POST /lessons/draft
x-holonograph-run-mode: production
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "kind": "fixture",
  "cluster": { /* cluster payload from the previous step */ },
  "parentSurfaceId": "classify-intent",
  "seedEventId": "evt_01H..."
}
```

        For `fixture` drafts, provide either a `seedEventId` (a real event to base the fixture on) or a `seedRawRequest` (a hand-authored request shape). Optionally supply a `parentFixtureId` if this fixture should stack on an existing one.

        Response: a `draft` object, an optional `classification` label the drafter applied, and an `enqueued` flag reflecting whether the draft was queued for the gate.

### 4. Approve or reject at the gate

        Approve:

```
POST /hil/approve
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "draftId": "draft_01H...",
  "approverId": "brian",
  "comment": "Correction verified against the surface's rules. Approving."
}
```

        Reject (a comment is required; the record of why matters):

```
POST /hil/reject
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "draftId": "draft_01H...",
  "approverId": "brian",
  "comment": "This one's not a pattern — the customer was testing us. Discarding."
}
```

        Both endpoints return the current `status` and a `history[]` of the actions taken on this draft so far.

### 5. Publish

        Once approved, publish the draft to make it live. Provide any existing lessons the publisher should consider superseding; the publisher will merge/replace/link as appropriate.

```
POST /lessons/publish
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "draftId": "draft_01H...",
  "candidateExistingLessonIds": ["lesson_01G..."]
}
```

        Response: a publish `report` naming the new artifact id, any superseded artifacts, and the substrate event the publish itself produced.

### Re-run a published fixture

        Once a fixture is live, you can re-run it any time against its parent surface:

```
POST /fixtures/rerun
Content-Type: application/json

{ "fixtureId": "fx_01H..." }
```

        Response includes the actual `result` the run produced and the `expected[]` assertions the fixture carries. The diff between the two is your regression signal.

## Reading the output

        Published artifacts become substrate. That means they show up as their own events, they get versioned, and, crucially, future drift readings can point at "this artifact was published on Tuesday" as a candidate explanation for a movement in the numbers.

        The pipeline is *recursive by construction*. The drafter's own model call passes through the lens, so the act of proposing a correction is itself observed. Getting better is a measured event.

## Reference

### Endpoints

Method & path	Purpose

`POST /hil/override`	Record a human override on a captured event.

`POST /lessons/cluster`	Cluster overrides in a window.

`POST /lessons/capture-scan`	Sweep judged failures on opt-in surfaces into the curation store so they cluster. Judged failures live in the event store and the clusterer reads the curation store; without this bridge a failure never clusters unless an override seeded it by hand. Opt in per surface with `captureJudgedFailures`. Idempotent per source event and dimension; the approver gate still gates the drafted lesson.

`POST /lessons/draft`	Ask the drafter to propose a corrective artifact for a cluster.

`POST /hil/approve`	Approve a draft at the gate.

`POST /hil/reject`	Reject a draft at the gate (comment required).

`POST /lessons/publish`	Publish an approved draft as substrate.

`POST /fixtures/rerun`	Re-run a published fixture against its parent surface.

### POST /hil/override: request

Field	Shape	Notes

`agentId`	string (req)	The agent this override applies to.

`surfaceId`	string (opt)	The surface, when known.

`correlationId`	string (opt)	Ties the override to the original call.

`tags`	string[] (opt)	Cohort tags like `fix_tier=…`, `severity=…`, and any other identifiers that will help clustering later.

`originalOutput`	object (req)	What the system produced.

`correctedOutput`	object (req)	What the human sent instead.

`rationale`	string (opt)	Human explanation of the correction.

`activeArtifacts`	array (opt)	Which lessons / fixtures were active at the time of the original call.

### POST /lessons/draft: request

Field	Shape	Notes

`kind`	enum (req)	`skill`, `lesson`, `fixture`, or `code-change-recommendation`.

`cluster`	object (req)	Payload from `/lessons/cluster`.

`enqueue`	boolean (opt)	Queue the draft for the gate immediately. Default true.

`parentSurfaceId`	string	Required for `fixture` drafts.

`seedEventId`	string (opt)	For `fixture`: base the fixture on a real event.

`seedRawRequest`	object (opt)	For `fixture`: hand-authored request shape when there's no seed event.

`parentFixtureId`	string (opt)	For `fixture`: stack this fixture on an existing one.

---

### Chapter 14 — Conformance & fixtures

_Permalink: https://holonograph.ai/guide/conformance_

Chapter 14

# Conformance & fixtures

        A capability surface is what you say your agent can do: the tools it exposes, the rules it should follow. Conformance turns that description into reproducible checks: a set of fixtures a scheduled run can execute, and a verdict that tells you whether each rule held. The flow is *derive → approve → check*.

## What it is

        Three moving pieces:

          - **The derive step** reads a capability surface (its tool declarations and prose rules) and proposes candidate fixtures, one per rule, each with the strongest assertion the rule allows.

          - **The fixtures step** is the human-in-the-loop approval gate. A named approver reviews the candidates, edits or discards, and commits the ones they trust. Nothing runs as a check until it's approved.

          - **The check step** runs the approved fixtures against real events over a window and returns a verdict per fixture plus a summary.

### Enforceability taxonomy

        Not every rule can be checked mechanically. The derive step labels each candidate with one of three enforceability categories, so the coverage report is honest about which rules the machine can actually hold you to:

Label	Meaning

`trace-enforceable`	The rule maps to a deterministic check on the captured trace: tool invocation, marker presence, output field.

`judge-required`	The rule can only be evaluated by a graded judgment call: an LLM judge running against the event.

`unenforceable`	The rule is worth stating but can't be mechanically checked at all (e.g. "be polite"). Recorded for completeness; produces no assertion.

## Why it matters

        A prose rule that can't be checked is a rule the system will drift on. Conformance moves rules from "our team believes this" to "the last check confirmed this at 06:00 Tuesday". The coverage report tells you exactly how many of the surface's rules you have mechanical accountability for, and the needs-repair panel tells you which ones the derive step couldn't formalize on its own.

## How to use it

### 1. Derive candidates from the surface

        Send the capability surface (its tools and its rules) and get back a set of candidate fixtures with per-rule enforceability labels.

```
POST /lens/conformance/derive
x-holonograph-run-mode: production
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "surfaceId": "classify-intent",
  "tools": [ /* tool declarations */ ],
  "rules": [
    "If the user asks for a refund, invoke the refund_lookup tool before responding.",
    "Never quote a specific dollar amount unless refund_lookup returned one.",
    "Be polite."
  ]
}
```

        The response gives you the candidates, a coverage summary (e.g. "2 of 3 rules mechanically enforceable"), and a needs-repair list for rules the derive step could not fully formalize.

### 2. Review and approve

        Each candidate is a JSON fixture describing an assertion (or a set of assertions, guarded by a `when` predicate). Review the derived shape, edit if needed, and submit each approved fixture with an `approverId`.

```
POST /lens/conformance/fixtures
x-holonograph-run-mode: production
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "approverId": "brian",
  "sourceSurfaceId": "classify-intent",
  "fixture": {
    "fixtureId": "refund-requires-lookup",
    "ruleId": "billing-triage-refund-flow-01",
    "ruleSource": "Refund rules v3",
    "description": "If the user asks for a refund, refund_lookup must be invoked before responding.",
    "enforceability": "trace-enforceable",
    "appliesTo": { "surfaceId": "classify-intent" },
    "when": [{ "kind": "marker-contains", "column": "user_message", "value": "refund" }],
    "assertion": { "kind": "marker-contains", "column": "tool_invocations", "value": "refund_lookup" }
  }
}
```

          The tool-discipline recipe
          The cleanest trace-enforceable realization of "tool X was invoked" is `marker-contains` on a consumer-emitted column. Your agent emits a delimited-list substrate column (here `tool_invocations`) recording every tool it actually called; the fixture checks that column with `marker-contains`. Deterministic, cheap, and consumer-neutral. It catches missed tool calls without an LLM judge.

        Response: an `eventId` for the approval event. The fixture is now live in the store and will be picked up by subsequent checks.

### 3. Run a check

        Point the checker at either an inline fixture or a stored one, plus a window and a surface filter.

```
POST /lens/conformance/check
x-holonograph-run-mode: production
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "fixtureId": "refund-requires-lookup",
  "surfaceId": "classify-intent",
  "since": "2026-07-01T00:00:00Z",
  "until": "2026-07-05T00:00:00Z"
}
```

        The response includes a top-level `verdict`, a per-event breakdown, the count of events checked, and the window actually used.

## Reading the output

        Conformance findings share the operator lifecycle described in
          [The attention spine](./attention-spine): one identity, one annotation trail, one path
          into a proposal.

### Assertion kinds

Kind	Shape	Passes when

`marker-contains`	`{ column, value }`	A delimited-list substrate column contains `value` as one of its comma-separated members. The consumer-neutral, trace-enforceable realization of "tool X was invoked" when the consumer captures invocations in a column.

`marker-not-contains`	`{ column, value }`	The delimited-list column does NOT contain `value`. Used for forbidden members.

`marker-present`	`{ column, equals? }`	A named substrate column is present on the event. Optionally, its value equals a fixed string.

`marker-absent`	`{ column }`	A named substrate column is absent from the event.

`tool-invoked`	`{ toolName }`	The named tool appears in the call trace. See the callout above: prefer `marker-contains` on a consumer-emitted column for tool-discipline enforcement.

`tool-not-invoked`	`{ toolName }`	The named tool does NOT appear in the call trace. A forbidden path.

`judge`	`{ prompt }`	An LLM judge is invoked with the given prompt and returns a pass/fail verdict against the event.

### Guarded assertions

        A fixture can carry a `when` predicate that decides whether the assertions apply to a given event. The predicate uses the same assertion kinds as the assertions themselves. If `when` is absent, the assertions apply to every event in the window.

```
{
  "fixtureId": "no-dollar-figures-without-lookup",
  "when": [{ "kind": "marker-not-contains", "column": "tool_invocations", "value": "refund_lookup" }],
  "assertion": { "kind": "marker-not-contains", "column": "response_text", "value": "$" }
}
```

        An event that fails the `when` predicate returns `not-applicable` for this fixture instead of pass/fail.

### Verdict precedence

        When multiple assertions run against one event, the overall event verdict is the strongest of the individual assertion verdicts, in this order:

          - `fail`: one assertion definitively failed.

          - `pass`: at least one assertion passed and none failed.

          - `requires-judge`: a `judge` assertion needs to be run before the verdict is complete.

          - `unevaluable`: the event was missing the shape needed to run the assertion at all.

          - `not-applicable`: the `when` guard filtered this event out.

        The check's top-level verdict is the strongest across events, using the same precedence.

### Coverage report

        The derive response's coverage summary is the honest headline: *K of N rules are mechanically enforceable*. It's the number to track over time. As your rules mature and the derive step's classifier improves, the ratio should climb. What it can't yet cover ends up in the needs-repair panel.

### Needs-repair panel

        A rule ends up in `needsRepair` when the derive step couldn't turn it into a check on its own, usually because the rule is ambiguous, or references a system state the fixture format doesn't reach yet. Two ways to clear the entry: rephrase the rule so the derive step can formalize it, or hand-author a fixture and approve it directly.

## Reference

### Endpoints

Method & path	Purpose

`POST /lens/conformance/derive`	Propose candidate fixtures from a capability surface.

`POST /lens/conformance/fixtures`	Approve a fixture (name an `approverId`).

`POST /lens/conformance/check`	Run one or more fixtures against events in a window.

### POST /lens/conformance/derive: response fields

Field	Shape	Notes

`surfaceId`	string	Echo of the surface.

`candidates[]`	array	Proposed fixtures, one per rule that could be formalized.

`coverage`	object	"K of N rules mechanically enforceable" summary.

`needsRepair[]`	array	Rules the derive step could not formalize.

`droppedCount`	number	Count of rules discarded outright (empty, duplicate, or unenforceable in a way the format can't record).

`readBy`	string	The identifier of the derive-step version that produced this output.

`clerkResponseIssue`	object (opt)	Present when the derive step's own output had a shape problem worth surfacing.

### POST /lens/conformance/check: request & response

Field	Shape	Notes

`fixture`	object (opt)	Inline fixture. One of `fixture` or `fixtureId` is required.

`fixtureId`	string (opt)	Stored fixture to run.

`surfaceId`	string (opt)	Restrict the check to one surface.

`provenance`	enum (opt)	Default `all`. Same values as [GET /lens/events](./snapshot).

`since`, `until`	ISO 8601 (opt)	Window bounds.

`limit`	number (opt)	Cap on events considered. Default 1000.

`verdict`	enum	Top-level: `pass`, `fail`, `requires-judge`, `unevaluable`, `not-applicable`.

`verdictDetails[]`	array	Per-event breakdown.

`checkedEventCount`	number	How many events were actually evaluated.

`window`	object	The actual window used (may differ from request when bounds were open).

### Chapter 15 — Rubric coverage and de-saturation

_Permalink: https://holonograph.ai/guide/rubric-coverage_

Chapter 15

# Rubric coverage and de-saturation

        One rubric over a population with real sub-kinds judges the union weakly, or judges the wrong specifics. This chapter is the loop that fixes that: scope a rubric per facet, see which facets have one, draft the ones that do not, and check that what you drafted can still tell a wrong answer from a right one.

## What it is

        A grading dimension carries one `rubricRef`. Point it at a surface whose population is heterogeneous, with members like `Daily Summary`, `Weather Advisory` and `Weekly Check-in`, and that one rubric either grades the union loosely or grades one member's specifics and mis-grades the rest.

        `rubricDispatch` scopes a rubric per facet without enumerating the members in the contract:

```
{
  "id": "signal-quality",
  "scoring": "llm-judge",
  "rubricRef": "gs://rubrics/signal-general.md",
  "rubricDispatch": {
    "facet": "signal.name",
    "refsFrom": "gs://rubrics/signal-alert/",
    "refs": { "Morning Routine": "gs://rubrics/pinned/morning.md" }
  }
}
```

Field	What it declares

`facet`	The cohort-tag key whose per-event value selects the rubric. It has to be a key in the surface's declared `cohortTags` vocabulary: a bounded identifier, not a human-authored display string with its em-dashes and emoji.

`refsFrom`	The bucket a per-facet rubric resolves from by convention. The rubric for value V is `refsFrom` + the normalized V + `.md`. Adding a member's rubric is a bucket write, never a contract change.

`refs`	Optional pins that override the convention for named values. Keys are matched in their normalized form, so pinning `Morning Routine` addresses the same rubric identity the convention would.

        The dimension's own `rubricRef` is re-cast as the required default. An unknown or unmatched facet is scored against it rather than skipped, because skipping would manufacture the judge-liveness hole the instrument exists to close. It is scored, marked, and counted.

### One normalization, shared

        A facet value and its filename have to address the same rubric, so both the dispatch and the drafter that writes the bucket file call one function. It folds Unicode and strips combining marks, lowercases, collapses every run of non-alphanumerics to a single hyphen, and trims:

```
"Morning Routine"                → morning-routine.md
"Weather — Heat Advisory ⚠️"      → weather-heat-advisory.md
"café"                           → cafe.md
```

        A value that is entirely non-alphanumeric, a bare emoji say, normalizes to nothing. That is an unaddressable stem, so the planner reads it as an unmatched value rather than pointing at a `.md` that cannot exist.

## Why it matters

        Two properties make the loop auditable rather than hopeful.

### The default is countable, and says why

        Every scored event is stamped with which rubric judged it and, when that was the default, why. Four reasons, and they are different problems:

Reason	What happened	What to do

`no-bespoke-ref`	A declared facet value with no per-facet rubric authored yet.	Nothing is wrong. This is the drafter's work queue.

`unmatched-value`	A `facet=value` tag was present, but the value is not declared and does not normalize to one.	A typo or an undeclared member. Fix the tag or declare the value.

`facet-tag-absent`	The event carried no `facet=` tag at all.	Un-tagged emit. Fix the producer.

`pin-unresolved`	An explicit `refs` pin was set and failed to load.	A bad pin. Louder than a convention miss, because you asked for this one by name.

        Without the split, the default population is one undifferentiated bucket and a coverage gap is indistinguishable from a broken emitter.

### The default vouches for less

        A default-scored event is also reduced-reach. The surface-general rubric vouches for surface-general correctness, not for domain quality, so it is deliberately strict about what it can see and silent about what it cannot. Scores under it are not comparable to scores under a bespoke rubric, and the lens treats the difference as a property of the instrument rather than of the agent.

## How to use it

### Read the worklist

```
GET /lens/facet-coverage?surfaceId=signal-alert
```

        One report per dispatching dimension. The counts are the readout: `facetsSeen` against `bespokeCount`, `scoredOnDefault` split by reason, `untaggedCount`, and `defaultOnly` for the facets that have never had anything but the default. `facets` carries the per-facet detail, each entry naming its `source` and, where that is `default`, its `defaultReason`.

        Re-derived per read from the apparatus columns. A surface with no dispatching dimension returns empty rather than zero.

### Draft one

```
POST /lens/rubric/propose
{
  "surfaceId": "signal-alert",
  "dimensionId": "signal-quality",
  "facetValue": "Morning Routine"
}
```

        The deterministic scaffold is assembled server-side from the contract: the dimensional-context header and the required verdict shape come from `rubricDispatch` and `judgeClaimContract`. The narrator contributes the domain grading criteria and nothing else. It has no channel through which to emit a number, so a fabricated threshold is structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely.

        The response carries the `refPath` the approved body belongs at, the `draft`, and two honesty flags. `narratorStatus` is `llm` when a real narrator produced the criteria, `stub` when none is configured, and `stub-fallback` when one was configured and threw: a draft returned under `stub-fallback` is a deterministic skeleton and must not read as an authored proposal. `evidenceAvailable` flags whether the count behind the draft was measured or is a placeholder.

        Propose-only. The draft goes to the approver gate, and the approved body is what the operator writes to the bucket. The lens never writes the rubric.

### Check that it discriminates

        A rubric can be authored, resolved, and scoring, and still be blind. If a value sits in the judge's sight and the rubric never asks about it, an output that is wrong along that value scores as if it were right. The score saturates.

```
POST /lens/saturation/audit
{
  "surfaceId": "signal-alert",
  "dimensionId": "signal-quality"
}
```

        The audit reads the dimension's declared `expectsGrounding` axes and, for each, computes the pass-rate of the declared misuse values against the dimension's `passThreshold`.

Per axis	Means

`blind`	The misuse passes at or above the blind threshold, 0.5 by default. The judge is letting it through.

`discriminating`	The misuse reliably fails.

`unverified`	Too few misuse samples, five by default, or no declared `passThreshold`. Honest-null, not a pass.

        The dimension's verdict is `saturated`, `discriminating`, `unverified`, or `no-expectation` where nothing was declared to check. Each axis also reports its misuse and correct-use counts, both pass-rates and the mean misuse score, because a working judge passes correct use and fails misuse, and seeing only one half of that is not evidence.

          Functional, not statistical
          An earlier version of this check asked whether the score varies with the axis at all, by analysis of variance. That is the wrong question. A judge scoring the misuse 8.4 against a correct 9 varies significantly and still passes the misuse. Separability is not adequate penalization. The verdict is the pass-rate, which is also robust to a judge catching some of the misuse for an unrelated reason: it still reads blind on the fraction it lets through.

        No judge is in the loop. The audit reads the substrate alone, because a saturated judge cannot be its own alarm. There is no approver gate and no model call. `provenance` defaults to `all`, so a replay panel built by varying the grounding is in scope, and `correlationIdPrefix` scopes the read to it.

### Fan out a focused reviewer

        Given measured saturation, the remedy is not to rewrite the holistic rubric. It is to add a reviewer that looks at one thing:

```
POST /lens/rubric/desaturate
{
  "surfaceId": "signal-alert",
  "dimensionId": "signal-quality",
  "facetValue": "Morning Routine",
  "blindDimension": {
    "name": "hrv-provenance",
    "description": "whether the HRV figure came from the overnight window it claims",
    "groundingKey": "hrv_metric_type",
    "misuseValues": ["intraday_spot"]
  },
  "saturationEvidence": {
    "scenarios": [
      { "label": "overnight (correct)", "judgeMean": 8.9 },
      { "label": "intraday spot (wrong)", "judgeMean": 8.4 }
    ],
    "replayRunRef": "replay:hrv-probe:"
  }
}
```

        You supply the measured evidence; the server drafts against it. The deterministic facts, the blind dimension and the saturation matrix and the fan-out structure, are pinned server-side, and the narrator writes the focused criteria only. The same discipline as `/propose`, and the same approver gate.

        What comes back is a focused sub-reviewer plus a registrable fan-out fragment: a separate `role: 'judge'` surface, its routing, and the `judgeSurfaceId` link that attaches it to the subject dimension. It appends. The holistic rubric is never replaced, because a focused judge that replaced it would trade one blind spot for another.

        Declaring `misuseValues` on the fan-out is what makes it auditable in turn. Omit them and the new judge is not saturation-auditable until you declare them.

          A misuse value is an output correlate
          The audit keys on the grounding value, so a declared misuse value only discriminates when it is a value the producer consumed that correlates with the wrong output. A value that labels the grounding *situation* instead admits both a faithful and a faulty output under the same value: the pass-rate mixes the two, lands near half, and mislabels the judge blind. Such an axis is auditable only when the events are scoped to the faulty arm first.

## Reading the output

        Three apparatus columns are stamped on every dispatched judgment. They are reserved, so a contract may not declare them.

Column	Carries

`judge.rubric_source`	`facet` or `default`.

`judge.rubric_facet`	The facet value the event dispatched on.

`judge.rubric_default_reason`	One of the four reasons, when the source was `default`.

          Which rubric an event got is instrument variance
          A default-scored population scores systematically lower for instrument reasons. Attributing that gap to the agent is the same mistake as attributing a regional confound to it. `judge.rubric_source` is a conditioning-permitted axis for exactly this reason, alongside the rubric hash, and the variance decomposition treats both as instrument variance rather than agent variance.

        Two of the attention spine's twenty-six sources file from here. `rubric-gap` is a declared facet riding the default with no bespoke rubric authored, and it mints an `author-rubric` proposal. `rubric-ref-broken` is a reference that no longer resolves, and it mints `fix-rubric-ref`. See [The attention spine](./attention-spine).

## Reference

### Endpoints

Method & path	Purpose

`GET /lens/facet-coverage`	The coverage readout per dispatching dimension, with the per-facet detail and the default split by reason.

`POST /lens/rubric/propose`	Draft a bespoke rubric for one named facet value. Propose-only, approver-gated.

`POST /lens/saturation/audit`	The judge-independent discrimination check against the declared grounding. Pure read.

`POST /lens/rubric/desaturate`	Draft a focused sub-reviewer plus its fan-out fragment, from measured saturation evidence. Propose-only, approver-gated.

### Contract surface

        `rubricDispatch`, `expectsGrounding`, `judgeSurfaceId` and `judgeClaimContract` are all declared on the grading dimension; see [What a dimension declares](./surface-contracts#what-a-dimension-declares). The dispatch decision is a published contract, shared by the lens's own gated judge and by an operator's inline one, so both resolve a facet to the same rubric. Resolving the rubric bytes is the caller's: the plan says what to fetch, the caller fetches, and the apparatus columns are stamped from the outcome.

        The drafter prompts and the composition order behind `/propose` and `/desaturate` ship inside the binary.

---

### Chapter 16 — Facet separability

_Permalink: https://holonograph.ai/guide/facet-separability_

Chapter 16

# Facet separability

        Fanning out to a focused judge per construct asserts, on faith, that those constructs are separable. This chapter is the certification under that assertion: whether a decomposition is a real topology, one axis wearing two names, or a prerequisite dressed as a peer.

## What it is

        Correlation is symmetric. It can say two facets move together; it cannot say that breaking A degrades B while breaking B leaves A intact. That asymmetry is the whole question, and it is invisible to any correlation-shaped measure, the [orthogonality audit](./variance-isolation) included.

        So the audit intervenes. Over a joint-state panel, events labelled by which facets' defects were injected, it runs a factorial and reads the directional cross-over-main ratio in each direction: how much facet F's score moves when F's own defect is injected, against how much it moves when G's is.

Verdict	Signature	What it means	What to do

`separable`	Both ratios low	Independent axes.	Keep both.

`collinear-collapse`	Both high, symmetric	One axis wearing two names.	Rejoin. This is the only verdict where rejoining is right.

`asymmetric-subsumption`	One high, one low	The high-ratio facet subsumes the low one: a prerequisite or constituent relationship, not a duplicate.	Keep both. The subsumed one is the sharp sub-dimension; the other is the catch-all.

`unverified`	Undersampled, a dead own-axis, or a compensatory coupling	Not established.	Nothing yet. Reported rather than rounded to separable.

          The trap this closes
          A saturation or collinearity signal on its own says "these look redundant, rejoin them." That is right for `collinear-collapse` and wrong for `asymmetric-subsumption`, where rejoining destroys a real, independently manipulable axis. Collinear behavior is a hypothesis. Run the factorial before you rejoin.

## Why it matters

        Two things depend on the answer being right.

        A fan-out is a claim about topology. Minting three focused judges per subject asserts those three constructs can be judged apart. If two of them are one axis, you have bought two judges' latency and cost for one axis of signal, and their agreement will read as corroboration when it is tautology.

        Reflection depends on it further downstream. Full orthogonality is one of the grant's hard preconditions, and a decomposition that has not certified cannot satisfy it. See [What has to hold before a cell reflects](./judge-modes#what-has-to-hold).

## How to use it

        Three reads, in order of cost. The screen proposes a hypothesis, the audit certifies it, the monitor watches it.

### Screen for candidates

```
POST /lens/redundancy/screen
{ "surfaceId": "classify-intent" }
```

        Over per-event score vectors it returns the pairwise collinearity matrix and, for each collinear pair, two things the matrix alone does not give: a scrap-pick naming which twin is the dependent copy, and a residual localization naming the substrate column that holds the copy's only independent variance. Omit `dimensionIds` and every scored dimension on the surface is screened.

        Data-gated. A pair below the minimum sample floor reads `undersampled` and a dimension with no variance reads `no-variance`, with a pointer at the saturation audit, since a dimension that never moves is usually a blind judge rather than a redundant one. The screen withholds rather than fires on a thin panel.

### Certify the pair

```
POST /lens/facet-topology/audit
{
  "surfaceId": "classify-intent",
  "facets": [
    { "dimensionId": "hrv-provenance",  "defectColumn": "defect.hrv",   "defectValue": "injected" },
    { "dimensionId": "place-identity",  "defectColumn": "defect.place", "defectValue": "injected" }
  ]
}
```

        Each `facets` entry is a panel-based expectation: the facet's score dimension, the diagnostic substrate column marking its injected defect, and the value that marks the defect as present. At least two are required, because the question is about a pair.

        `provenance` defaults to `all`, so a replay or emitted panel is in scope, and `correlationIdPrefix` scopes to one. `options` takes the cell-size floor and the ratio cutoffs where a surface needs them; the defaults are conservative.

        Read-only, so propose-only. The audit returns a verdict per unordered pair and the operator promotes the split, keeps it, or rejoins.

          The audit inherits its panel's validity
          A facet whose own injected defect does not actually move its own score makes the cross-over-main ratio explode into a fake subsumption. Those pairs are reported as such rather than scored. The factorial is only as good as the ablation underneath it: if the defect you injected was not a defect, nothing downstream of it is a measurement.

### Watch the band

```
POST /lens/pairwise-monitor/run
{ "surfaceId": "classify-intent" }
```

        The factorial is expensive and offline. The monitor is the cheap online guard on it. Over per-event defect co-firing it returns, per dimension pair, the co-trigger contingency and the marginal-adjusted phi coupling, which is the measure that disentangles real coupling from a shared score floor, plus the signal for a pair collapsing toward collinear while live.

        Give it the characterized band as `expectedBands` and it returns a drift verdict proposing a re-run of the audit. Run the audit with `persist: true` and it closes the loop itself: the audit also runs the monitor over the same window and appends a durable characterization record merging the verdict with the co-trigger band per pair, which is what the monitor reads back. `bandTolerance` sets the band's half-width, 0.1 by default.

        The monitor proposes drift. It never adjusts a band, because a band that moves itself measures nothing.

### When the judge and the producer disagree

```
POST /lens/contested-cohort/screen
{ "surfaceId": "classify-intent", "dimensionId": "correctness" }
```

        The adjacent question, converging on the same fields. For one judged dimension it partitions events by each candidate substrate-column cohort and tests whether the judge's fail-rate on a cohort value is systematically elevated against the rest of the population, by a two-by-two chi-square per cohort with the family under false-discovery control.

        A contested cohort is one where the producer's outputs are systematically rejected. It is reported with the producer's own within-cohort consistency alongside, because a producer that is consistently doing one thing and consistently marked down for it has a different shape from one that is erratic.

        The lens cannot adjudicate which party is right, and does not try. It points at the interaction, notes that a focused judge on that field would isolate it, and routes to review. Cohorts below the sample floor are withheld.

## Reading the output

        Every read here is read-only and propose-only, and three of the attention spine's sources file from them: `redundancy-candidate`, which mints a `rejoin-dimension` proposal, plus `pairwise-drift` and `contested-cohort`, which mint nothing. A source with no default proposal is one where the remedy is a judgment the lens declines to make for you.

        All four are data-gated and report honest nulls. A withheld pair, an undersampled cohort and an unverified verdict are all distinguishable from a clean result, which is the property that makes a quiet report worth anything.

## Reference

### Endpoints

Method & path	Purpose

`POST /lens/redundancy/screen`	The collinearity matrix, with a scrap-pick and residual localization per collinear pair.

`POST /lens/facet-topology/audit`	The interventional factorial. Returns a verdict per unordered pair; `persist: true` also records the characterization and its band.

`POST /lens/pairwise-monitor/run`	The online guard: co-trigger contingency, marginal-adjusted phi, and a drift verdict against the characterized band.

`POST /lens/contested-cohort/screen`	Cohorts where the judge systematically rejects the producer, with the producer's within-cohort consistency.

### Where this sits

        Upstream is [Rubric coverage and de-saturation](./rubric-coverage): a de-saturation fan-out creates the facets this chapter certifies, so the two run as one loop rather than two tools. Alongside it at axis altitude is the orthogonality audit in [Variance isolation](./variance-isolation), which asks whether a declared substrate column explains anything, a different object measured a different way.

        The factorial, the coupling measure and the tuning constants ship inside the binary. The verdict vocabulary and the record shapes are public contract.

---

### Chapter 17 — Judge modes and reflection

_Permalink: https://holonograph.ai/guide/judge-modes_

Chapter 17

# Judge modes and reflection

        Every judge/gate relationship on a surface is one of four modes, the valid cells of two independent questions: does the producer wait for the verdict, and may the verdict touch delivery. Reflection is the third cell, and the only one Holonograph grants rather than leaving to configuration.

## What it is

        Two axes. **Timing** is `async` (the judge runs off the producer's hot
          path) or `inline` (the producer waits for the verdict before finishing).
          **Authority over delivery** runs `open` (observe only) to
          `reflection` (the judge may send the producer back to retry) to `gate`
          (delivery is blocked).

	open	reflection	gate

**async**	Open, asynchronous	impossible	impossible

**inline**	Open, inline	Reflection granted	Actually gated

        The two empty cells are impossible rather than unspecified. Reflection and gating both need the
          verdict before the producer finishes, and an asynchronous verdict is not back yet. The
          consequence is worth stating plainly: **async is available only to a judge that observes
          and nothing more.**

## Why it matters

### The judge never disposes

        Across all four modes the judge's authority stops at reflection. It can observe, and at most it
          can send the producer back to try again. It cannot block delivery. Disposal belongs to
          deterministic code in the gate, which is producer-owned, or to operator policy. Propose-only
          holds in every mode.

### Inline and observing is the expensive cell

        A judge that runs in-request while its verdict touches nothing pays full latency for no in-band
          effect. A fleet of observe-only judges parked there is where large latency overheads come from.
          The cell is justified as a step toward reflection or a gate, not as a destination. Move the judge
          to async, or give it authority.

## How to use it

          - Pick the mode per surface. A judge that only records belongs in async.

          - Reflection is a capped retry, not a block. Budget the retries.

          - A gate is deterministic code reading a verdict. Write the gate; do not ask the model to be one.

## Reading the output

        An asynchronous verdict lands after the producer has answered, as a linked judge event. A reader
          resolves it link-first and falls back to the embedded verdict, fail-open, so a consumer never
          blocks on a verdict that has not arrived. Per-judgment verdict provenance distinguishes the raw
          judge result from the producer-filtered one.

## Why reflection is gated

        Reflection turns a judge from an evaluator you read into an optimization target the producer
          chases. That inverts the trust requirement. A judge you only read can be a little wrong, because
          you flag and a human reviews. A judge you optimize against has to be right, because the producer
          will find and exploit every gap in it.

        The gate is on validity, not on discrimination. Those come apart: a judge can score stably and
          still be blind, saturated, or wrong about how a construct should treat absence. Scoring the same
          way every time is reliability, and reliability does not imply validity.

### The specific hazard

        Real dimensions are often requires-confirmation: an honest "I do not have the data" correctly
          scores low. Put that judge in a retry loop and the cheapest way for the producer to raise its
          score is to stop being honest about the absence and fabricate. That is the exact failure the
          apparatus exists to catch, now with a loop optimizing toward it.

        So reflection without established authority is not merely a waste of tokens and time. It is a
          pressure applied to the one behavior you most need preserved.

## What has to hold before a cell reflects

        Reflection unlocks for a `judge &times; rubric &times; facet &times; surface` cell when
          all of the following hold. The gate is dual: Holonograph computes the statistical pass, then a
          human confirms.

          - **Soak.** Enough live production data to reach a statistical N. Holonograph determines the statistical pass; a human approves the N, judging whether the sample spans the breadth of real inputs and outputs.

          - **Discrimination.** The facet's dimensions pass discrimination evaluation, with a human confirming key outlier calls and a statistical sampling of calls on that facet.

          - **Saturation cleared.** Every dimension passes the saturation audit, which is [a read you can run yourself](./rubric-coverage#the-saturation-audit).

        Validity is cell-specific, so the grant is too. A judge certified on one facet of one surface has
          said nothing about another.

## What reflection does

        A failing response returns to the producer with the judge's grounded critique attached, and the
          producer retries, capped. Reflection is the soft tier of the judge's authority over delivery: it
          can send the producer back, it cannot block. Blocking remains deterministic code in the gate, or
          operator policy.

## Revocation

        The grant is revoked on any change to the identity it was computed on. A new judge model, a
          revised rubric, a changed context scope: the cell certifies again or it does not reflect. This is
          the authority machinery applied to the judge rather than to the producer, and it suspends the same
          way for the same reasons.

## The shared-frame check

        One of those preconditions has an instrument of its own. Groundedness has to hold on both sides: a judge that read a different frame from the producer is not measuring the producer, and a groundedness alarm on such a pair points at the wrong party.

```
POST /lens/co-groundedness/screen
{ "surfaceId": "classify-intent" }
```

        Over the surface's claim-instrumented judged dimensions it classifies each judge-to-subject frame relation:

Relation	What it says

`shared-frame-intact`	Judge and producer were grounded in the same values. A groundedness finding here is about the producer.

`judge-misread-frame`	The judge read the frame wrong. The finding is about the judge.

`judge-frame-truncated`	The judge saw part of the frame. Its verdict is scoped to what it saw, whatever it asserts.

`judge-grounded-outside-frame`	The judge grounded on something the producer never had. It is marking the producer down for an absence that was never the producer's.

`not-assessable`	The relation could not be established. Reported rather than assumed intact.

        The last two are the observer-groundedness asymmetry, and they are the disambiguation to run before treating a groundedness alarm as a producer fault. Deterministic per verdict, certain or abstain: no false-discovery gate and no data floor, because each relation is established or it is not. Read-only, so it proposes and the operator disposes.

## Reference

Method & path	Purpose

`POST /lens/co-groundedness/screen`	Classify the judge-to-subject frame relation per claim-instrumented dimension.

        Your own reflection loop remains yours to run; nothing here prevents it. The claim is narrower: a retry loop against an uncertified judge spends tokens to apply pressure in an unknown direction. Holonograph turns reflection on when the cell has qualified, if you have asked for it.

        The taxonomy is the design of record for the judge/gate relationship and is documented ahead of
          the implementation. The reflection path and the judge-gate enforcement cluster each have their
          own specification; this chapter is the frame that places them.

---

### Chapter 18 — Seams

_Permalink: https://holonograph.ai/guide/seams_

Chapter 18

# Seams

        A value whose meaning is not fixed by its representation, driving a decision that governs a consequential transition, is a seam. It is permanent. You can close it and you can monitor it. You cannot validate it away.

## What it is

        A seam is an edge: the path a value travels from where it is produced to the decision that
          consumes it. Write it `I &rarr; DP`, interpretive source to decision point.

        Whether an input is interpreted is a property of that edge, not of the field and not of whether
          the code is deterministic. The same field can lie on a deterministic edge to one consumer and an
          interpreted edge to another. A model output, a classifier, an approximate match, a pattern applied
          to free text, an external feed, a recorded human judgment: each is an interpreted source, and each
          is interpreted because of what the consuming decision does with it.

        The decision point reverts to an ordinary, inert sink under one condition only: it stops making
          decisions. Its output goes to a log line, a rendered field, a return nobody branches on. Short of
          that, the seam stays.

## Why it matters

### Provenance is monotone

        Consider a decision that reads free text and returns one of three values:

        function decide(ticket): 'page' | 'auto-reply' | 'queue' {
  const msg = (ticket.subject + ticket.body).toLowerCase();   // I0
  if (INCIDENT.test(msg)) return 'page';
  ...
}

const action = decide(ticket);        // I1: deterministic in value, interpreted in provenance
if (action === 'page') pageOnCall();  // dispatch on I1 reaches authority

          The enum is not a sanitizer. It is the decision's codomain. `action` is a first-class
          interpretive value, deterministic in what it holds and interpreted in where it came from. The
          chain runs `I0 &rarr; DP &rarr; I1 &rarr; DP1` and onward, and the provenance rides
          through every hop. Relocating the decision upstream moves the decision point; it does not escape
          anything. The next scan finds it in its new place.

### Validation changes the character of the error, not its existence

        A schema boundary filters the catastrophic: wrong type, missing field, malformed JSON. It passes
          the shape-valid-but-wrong. So it raises the floor and, in the same motion, makes the residual
          error insidious, because the value now looks right, types right, and fails quietly downstream.

        A pattern that pulls `'success'` out of *"I hope you are a great success in life"*
          and resolves it to `route.SUCCESS` is the whole problem in one line. The enum fixed the
          form, not the misread. It is a confidently wrong signal wearing a valid badge.

        This is why structure cannot finish the job. Closing a seam makes the decision attended and
          monitorable. It does not make the decision correct. Correctness is a different axis, the empirical
          misfire rate, and the only instrument for it is soak. Structure hands off exactly the error class
          it cannot catch to the instrument that can.

## Open and closed

        With provenance carried, the two states have a precise inductive definition over the chain.

State	Condition

**closed**	The decision point is attended, meaning it has a defined no-match or abstention path, *and* its output's provenance chain terminates in non-deciding sinks. Every downstream consumer is either another closed decision point or something that does not decide.

**open**	Any unattended decision point in the chain, or a chain that feeds an unattended authority decision point. The defective state.

        A closed seam is a declared surface. It stays closed only while its measurement holds, which is
          why closed and ready for soak belong in the same breath.

## The four closure shapes

        These are the structural forms a closure takes. They are shapes, not an exhaustive list of the
          decisions that can exercise authority; the sink taxonomy is an open registry.

Shape	Form

`regex-over-value`	A pattern tested, matched or replaced against the interpreted value.

`branch-on-value`	An `if` or `switch` comparing the value to literals.

`threshold-on-value`	An `if` comparing the value to a numeric literal.

`value-as-key`	The value used as an index or map key.

## Model calls are seams

        A model call is a seam whose interpreter is not stationary. A pattern does not rewrite itself
          between releases; a model can be re-routed behind an unchanged alias, and the instrument scoring
          it is usually another model. So a model seam carries more variance machinery: the four-source
          decomposition, the served-model axis, judge facets, saturation and orthogonality.

        The machinery differs; the lifecycle does not. Code seams and model seams both soak, both file
          findings on the spine, and both reach authority. They sit on adjacent surfaces, not in separate
          systems. A seam is itself a light source, recorded as
          `seam//`, which is how a non-model interpreter takes the
          same slot a vendor would without pretending to be one.

## Reference

        The shape is the lens's own `judge &rarr; verdict &rarr; gate &rarr; action` model
          applied inside ordinary code: `decide &rarr; enum &rarr; dispatch &rarr; sink` is the
          same structure. The enum is a verdict, carrying light from an interpreted source, and a dispatch
          acting on it is governed by that light.

---

### Chapter 19 — The seam monitor

_Permalink: https://holonograph.ai/guide/seam-monitor_

Chapter 19

# The seam monitor

        The monitor has a build-time half and a run-time half over one record. Source analysis produces evidence, a gate adjudicates it, a confirmed seam is registered as a surface, and soak measures whether the closure holds against real inputs.

## What it is

        Five stages, each with one job and one output. The separation matters: the scanner is an evidence
          producer, not an adjudicator.

Stage	Role	Output

Source scan	Evidence producer	A candidate interpretation edge, as structural facts

Interpretation gate	Semantic adjudication	A typed disposition

Registration	Declaration	A surface on the append-only record

Run-time producer	Viability measurement	Soak findings on live traffic

Authority state	Consumer	The per-surface reading over all of the above

        The scan reports what it can establish structurally: that a value originates from a known source
          locus, flows through named identifiers, reaches a branch, threshold, pattern or key sink, and that
          the default path has a particular shape. It never emits a verdict.

### The three dispositions

        The gate answers one question before the authority machine asks any of its own: is this a closure
          over an open interpreted domain at all?

Disposition	Meaning

`certain-interpreted`	The input's meaning is not fixed by its representation and the edge governs authority. A real seam; the state machine applies.

`certain-mechanical`	The edge is deterministic or the domain is closed. An exact match, an enum lookup. Not a seam.

`unresolved`	Abstain. The apparatus cannot yet tell, so it withholds the disposition and keeps measuring.

        Only `certain-interpreted` edges become registered records. Abstention here means
          withholding a consequential disposition and continuing to measure. It is not a queue of requests
          for a human.

## Why it matters

### The scanner is its own dark surface

        Finding seams is itself a closure over an open domain, namely arbitrary code, so it reports its
          own blind spots as first-class coverage rather than as silence.

          - `coverage.status`: the overall coverage state for the scanned unit.

          - `coverage.supported_constructs`: the language constructs the front end actually handles.

          - `coverage.unresolved_edges`: edges the taint could not fully follow.

          - `coverage.unparsed`: code the front end could not parse.

          - `coverage.dynamic_escape`: points where dynamic dispatch, reflection or serialization broke the path.

        Partial coverage is never reported as no seams. A scan that could not follow an edge says so, and
          the hook that reports into a build session says so too rather than issuing a false all-clear.

### Propose only

        The monitor flags and drafts. It does not edit code and it does not block on the lens's own
          authority. Whether a build stops is a policy the operator or CI sets, and the detector must
          qualify before that policy is even eligible: observe first, everywhere, including the detector
          run against its own repository.

        The criterion that governs that qualification is the one the invariant demands of every other
          instrument. Under rising uncertainty the detector must abstain more, not assert more.

## How to use it

          - Scan a repository and push its seams to the lens, or run the hook so a seam is reported into the session that wrote it.

          - `--propose-sinks` and `--propose-skips` mechanically propose candidates for the authority-sink and skip-path lists rather than asking you to author them cold.

          - Accepted declarations are honored: a seam you declare drops from the lens as well as from the scan.

          - Each reported seam names the authority sink it reaches, so the choice is to declare it or restructure around it.

## Soak: the run-time half

        A soak is the empirical life of a registered seam: how often its no-match or abstention path
          actually fires, which branch it takes, how the decided value's identity churns over time, and
          optionally whether that value is efficacious.

        A soak observation is a full evaluation event rather than a new event kind, so every existing
          tool works on it unchanged: the producers, the dashboard, retention and husking, the judge link.
          The seam-ness lives on the run-time configuration axes instead.

Axis	Value

`provenance`	`seam`. The isolation key. It sits in neither the production-state nor the exploratory-state set, so soaks are excluded from every default analysis and cannot drown a small agent's readings.

`runMode`	The shared enum. Isolation is provenance-keyed and independent of run mode, so `eval` and `replay` mean here what they mean everywhere.

`lightSourceIdentifier`	`seam//`. A seam is a light source that is not a model, and it takes the slot honestly rather than faking a vendor.

        The husk-surviving facts, whether it abstained and which path it took and the value fingerprint,
          ride in the surface dimension, the substrate columns and the cohort tags. A raw decided value
          rides in the payload and husks away like a judge rationale.

## Reading the output

        Soaks file under one reserved surface, adjacent to the surface registered seams file under, with
          individual seams as loci inside it. Findings from both reach the attention spine as
          `builder-seam` and `seam-soak` sources, alongside every other finding the
          instrument produces.

## Reference

### Endpoints

Method & path	Purpose

`POST /lens/builder-seams`	The scanner pushes its current registered-seam set. Replace-current: a scan run is a complete re-derivation of the code's interpreted seams, so the newest push is the truth and a seam that no longer appears is gone. Writes the evidence registry only, never the contract registry. Returns `202 { accepted }` once the write is durable and visible to other instances. `501` where the registry is not wired, which is the only opt-in.

`GET /lens/builder-seams`	Confirm an ingest landed and is visible cross-instance before its call events start carrying a call-site id. A per-source summary by default; `?full=1` returns the held scans.

`POST /lens/seam-soak/judge`	Run the offline value-efficacy judge over a seam's stored raw-output corpus. Operator-invoked, approver and cost gated. The judge runs over the stored corpus, never the live stream, and verdicts are minted server-side on the judge surface. `501` where no judge scorer is wired.

        The shared vocabulary, the four sink shapes, the default-path forms and the sink kinds, lives in
          the public contract package so the build-time scanner and the run-time producer name the same
          things. The interpretation disposition is the same enum the authority state machine reads.

---

### Chapter 20 — The attention spine

_Permalink: https://holonograph.ai/guide/attention-spine_

Chapter 20

# The attention spine

        Every observe-only surface produces findings, and there are twenty-six sources of them. The spine gives all of them one operator lifecycle instead of one list per surface, and it is the substrate the authority state reads.

## What it is

        A cross-source triage layer over findings. It declares three objects and nothing else:

Object	What it holds

`FindingRef`	The stable identity of a finding, independent of the scan that produced it.

`TriageRecord`	An append-only annotation about that finding.

`Proposal`	What a confirmed finding mints into Curate.

### The sources

        Twenty-six, spanning judge behavior, evaluation structure, coverage, attribution, the store, and
          the seam work. They are listed here because the spine is only as good as what files into it.

Group	Sources

Judge behavior	`verdict-reliability`, `judge-liveness`, `judge-malfunction`, `co-groundedness`

Evaluation structure	`orthogonality-hypothesis`, `primary-axis-orthogonality`, `redundancy-candidate`, `pairwise-drift`, `contested-cohort`, `rubric-gap`, `rubric-ref-broken`

Coverage and reach	`coverage-gap`, `reach-gap`, `emission-gap`, `dark-mass-blindspot`, `read-window-underpowered`

Surface lifecycle and attribution	`trajectory`, `quarantine-candidate`, `retirement-candidate`, `hash-provenance`, `source-conflation`

Seams and authority	`builder-seam`, `seam-soak`, `authority-suspended`

Store	`store-capacity`, `retention-integrity`

        A code seam and a model call file into the same spine. They arrive from different sources and sit
          on adjacent surfaces, and from the lifecycle's side they are the same object.

### One surface, several agents

        When several of a swarm's agents emit onto one surface, pooling them is sometimes right and sometimes fabricates a statistic. Every source declares which, so a new producer cannot pool two agents by omission.

Partition	Behavior

`per-source`	Pooling corrupts the statistic or destroys attribution, so the source runs once per agent and each finding is stamped with its `sourceId`. A no-op where one surface has one agent. The analytic reads over scores and variance sit here: pooling two score populations manufactures correlation that neither agent shows.

`pooled-examine`	Pooling is correct, because the instrument is shared, the contract is global, or the grouping is the operator's and not the lens's to override. The `source-conflation` alarm watches these for a hidden per-agent split and surfaces it without imposing a partition.

`pooled`	Global, or keyed on a different axis entirely: the consumer's agent id, the rubric, the lens's own store. A per-agent split is not meaningful and the alarm ignores it.

        `source-conflation` is the twenty-sixth source and the one that reads the others: it compares agents inside a pooled read and reports where a single number is hiding two populations. It points, it does not repartition. Whether an operator's grouping is wrong is the operator's call.

### Three grains

        What a finding's identity means depends on its grain: `run` for one call,
          `conversation` for one conversation, and `structural` for a declared
          surface, dimension or axis with no single event behind it.

## Why it matters

        Two invariants hold the spine apart from the measurement it annotates.

### A triage annotation never reaches the substrate

        An annotation is *about* a derived finding. It lives in a separate store, downstream of
          derivation. It is never an input to the lens hash, and it never mutates the substrate, a prompt,
          or a threshold. The spine proposes; the existing gated approver path disposes. A triage click
          changes nothing on the lens.

### Identity survives re-derivation

        Findings are re-derived on every scan. A triage record therefore keys to a content-derived
          `findingKey` rather than a per-scan row index. Keying to a row index would orphan
          every annotation on the next deploy. `clusterId` stays an attribute, never the
          primary grain, because a non-deterministic key has the same effect.

## How to use it

          - Read findings from the spine rather than per-surface. One queue, one lifecycle.

          - Annotate a finding to record what triage concluded. Annotations accumulate; nothing is overwritten.

          - Mint a proposal from a confirmed finding. The proposal enters the approver path as a proposal, not as a change.

### Read the queue

```
GET /lens/attention?surfaceId=classify-intent&state=untriaged&severity=alarm&limit=50
Authorization: Bearer
x-holonograph-run-mode: production
```

        Filters: `surfaceId`, `source`, `state`, `severity`, `sort`, `since`, `until`, `limit`, `cursor`. Severity is one of `alarm`, `needs-review` or `coverage`, which is the ranking the default sort uses.

        Each item carries `findingRef` and its derived `findingKey`, the `source`, the `severity`, a `count` of the events that collapsed into it, `firstSeen` and `lastSeen`, the inline `evidence`, the derived `triageState`, the `latestTriage` record, `how`, and `gate`.

          The queue reads without a triage store
          Without a triage store wired, the queue still returns: every finding reads as untriaged. Writes are what need the store, and `POST /lens/attention/triage` answers `501` without one. An unconfigured deployment loses the lifecycle, not the observability.

### Open one finding

```
GET /lens/attention/evidence?findingKey=
```

        The decision-grade detail behind one row, fetched when an operator opens it rather than for every row in the queue. It returns a representative `exemplar`, the most recent flagged call in the class, with the prompt, the model's answer, the judge's verdict and rationale, and the mechanical claims: the tool the judge said was not invoked, the datum it said was fabricated. Alongside it, `sampleCount` and a `samples` list to spot-check, plus `reAdjudicable` and `unavailable`. Re-derived per read; nothing is persisted. A class that no longer recurs in the window returns an honest-null exemplar rather than a stale one.

### Annotate

```
POST /lens/attention/triage
Authorization: Bearer
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "findingRef": { "primary": { "grain": "structural", "id": "..." }, "attributes": { ... } },
  "disposition": "confirmed-defect",
  "rationale": "the judge passed three misuse samples in a row",
  "approverId": "brian"
}
```

        `rationale` and `approverId` are required: an annotation without a reason or an author is not a compliance record. Two optional fields pin what the operator saw, `evidenceSnapshotRef` for the denormalized slice and `asOf` for the substrate instant, so a decision stays reconstructible after the evidence moves on. The server stamps `occurredAt` itself.

### Three dispositions, five states

        A disposition is what the operator wrote. A state is what the queue derives.

Value	Kind	Meaning

`confirmed-defect`	disposition	Adjudicated real. This is the one that mints a proposal.

`false-alarm`	disposition	Adjudicated not real.

`acknowledged`	disposition	Real and accepted: a known blind spot the operator chooses to leave. Parked, not dismissed.

`untriaged`	state only	No record yet.

`resolved`	state only	The proposal was applied through Curate, or the finding stopped recurring. A lifecycle signal sets it, never a triage click.

### What a confirmed finding mints

        Twelve authoring targets. Each lands in Curate approver-gated, carrying intent rather than an apply-payload: the operator authors the change.

Proposal kind	Default source	The remedy

`grounding-cap-bump`	`verdict-reliability`	Raise the grounding cap the flagged verdicts are hitting.

`gate-dimension`	`judge-liveness`	Put a dimension under a gate.

`adjust-threshold`	operator-raised	Move a `passThreshold`.

`predicate-downweight`	`trajectory`	Downweight a trajectory predicate that over-fires.

`declare-axis`	`orthogonality-hypothesis`	Declare an emitted-but-undeclared column as its own axis. Splits a confound out.

`rejoin-dimension`	`redundancy-candidate`	Collapse a dependent dimension into the twin it duplicates. The inverse of `declare-axis`: this merges a copy back into the axis it never left.

`retire-surface`	`coverage-gap`, `retirement-candidate`	Retire a surface, or mark it forward-declared.

`release-from-quarantine`	`quarantine-candidate`	Release a quarantined stream.

`author-rubric`	`rubric-gap`	Author a bespoke per-facet rubric for a facet that has only ridden the default.

`fix-rubric-ref`	`rubric-ref-broken`	Repair a rubric reference that no longer resolves.

`author-fixture`	operator-raised	Author a fixture the surface is missing.

`retention-policy`	`store-capacity`, `read-window-underpowered`	Adopt or tighten a retention preset. The operator sets the policy; the lens never compacts on its own.

        Fourteen of the twenty-six sources mint nothing by default, `source-conflation` among them. A source with no default proposal is not a lesser finding: it is one where the remedy is a judgment the lens declines to pre-empt.

## Reading the output

        A finding carries its `findingRef`, the surface and dimension it came from, the run
          mode it was derived under, and its triage state. Where a finding has an exemplar, the exemplar
          payload travels with it under the same husk projection used elsewhere in the store, so a triaged
          finding on a compacted span still opens.

## What sits on top

        The spine is the base. Authority is a reading over the same record: a per-surface state derived
          from what the gates, the dependencies and the soak evidence say, re-derived on every read. A
          surface whose grant is withdrawn files `authority-suspended` back onto the spine as
          another finding, which is how a withdrawal reaches the same queue as everything else.

        Reflection sits above that again, switched on for a cell once its authority is established.

## Reference

### Endpoints

Method & path	Purpose

`GET /lens/attention`	The cross-source queue: findings merged with triage state, severity-ranked, cursor-paginated.

`GET /lens/attention/evidence`	The exemplar and sample list behind one finding.

`POST /lens/attention/triage`	Append one annotation. `501` without a triage store.

`GET /lens/trajectory-findings`	The `trajectory` source read on its own: the turn-to-conversation axis a per-turn judge structurally cannot see. Groups events by the consumer's boundary column, runs the detectors, and returns the findings alongside the honest-null accounting (events with no boundary key, turns with no output text, which predicates actually ran) so an unmeasured slice never reads as clean.

        All three are also served under the `/holonograph` alias. The reads derive per request and persist nothing; the write touches the triage store only, which is not an input to the lens hash.

        The public module declares the wire and store contract only. Which surface maps to which
          `FindingRef`, and the store implementation, live in the lens package.

---

### Chapter 21 — Authority

_Permalink: https://holonograph.ai/guide/authority_

Chapter 21

# Authority

        Authority is a state held per decision surface: the declared prerequisites for a specified consequential transition are satisfied on the record as it stands. It is established only by the satisfaction of the gates its contract names, it is re-derived at every read, and no actor confers it.

## What it is not

        Four neighbouring words get used for this and none of them is it.

Term	What it means

Permission	An actor is allowed to act.

Approval	An actor affirmatively accepts something.

Correctness	A proposition matches an applicable reference.

Confidence	A degree of belief, or a measurement's precision.

**Authority**	The declared prerequisites for this transition are satisfied on the record.

        Humans, builders and mechanicals all produce events on the record. No kind of actor confers
          authority. An operator approving a decision is approval, recorded as such; it does not move the
          state.

## The six states

        An ordered ladder a decision surface climbs, plus the one state the apparatus can drop it into.

State	Meaning

`unmapped`	No authority sink has been identified here. The honest default: not yet mapped, rather than no seam.

`mapped`	A sink is identified, but nothing asserts authority over it. The seam exists; no claim of certainty stands on it.

`declared`	Authority is asserted and the gate is live, but the certainty condition is not established and no qualifying evidence is accruing.

`qualifying`	Asserted and actively accumulating the evidence that would establish the condition. Live traffic is exercising the sink.

`granted`	The declared certainty condition is established on live evidence and every dependency holds.

`suspended`	Authority was granted and a dependency left its declared condition, so the apparatus withdrew the grant itself.

        Default ordering puts `suspended` first, because a grant withdrawn out from under a
          live decision is the loudest thing on the page. `granted` and `unmapped` are
          the quietest: one is working as intended, the other is a coverage note rather than an alarm.

### Re-derived, never stored

        A reading is computed from the recorded events at every read. No state is stored, so a reading
          cannot drift from the substrate it describes. A reading also never mutates anything: the apparatus
          proposes, the operator and CI dispose.

## The authority stack and its conditions

        Every object whose identity or value a grant was computed on is recorded as a stamped column. The
          set of them is the surface's authority stack. Where a dependency is a model, the recorded identity
          is the one that *served* the call, not the one requested.

        Each dependency declares the envelope within which a change leaves the grant valid.

Condition	Envelope

`identity`	The default. The dependency must be the same thing.

`equivalence`	A different thing, declared equivalent.

`reach`	Within a declared reach.

`band`	Within a declared band.

        A change inside the envelope is recorded and raised for review, with no transition. A change
          outside it suspends. Re-establishing a withdrawn grant takes the re-satisfaction of every gate
          over the post-change record, not an acknowledgement.

### Tears

        A tear is a served or judge model value appearing on a surface for the first time. The soak window
          anchors at the previous stack change, held back to the segment before the latest unacknowledged
          tear, and **a tear never self-clears**. An operator acknowledgement releases it; the
          window then starts no earlier than the acknowledged tear, and the acknowledgement leaves an
          append-only, server-minted audit record that is never compacted.

        Acknowledgements apply oldest first. Acknowledging a tear while an older one on the same surface
          is still open is refused. The operator's authority policy sets whether one acknowledgement covers
          a per-surface watermark, the default, or only the single tear.

## How to use it

          - Declare the surface and its contract: what the decision concludes, on what evidence, under what prerequisites, with which abstention path and gate composition.

          - Let it run. A surface without traffic cannot accumulate the evidence that would qualify it, which is why `declared` and `qualifying` are different states.

          - Read the map rather than a single number. A living system holds authority on every surface rarely and briefly; which surfaces hold it, and what withdrew the rest, is the reading.

## Reference

### Endpoints

Method & path	Purpose

`GET /lens/authority`	One reading per gated dimension, plus an honest `unmapped` reading for every gate-less surface. Re-derived per read.

`GET /lens/authority/tears`	The open tears on each surface, the acknowledgement records, and the granularity in force.

`POST /lens/authority/tear/acknowledge`	Acknowledge one tear. Body: `surfaceId`, `approverId`, optional `tearEventId` and `note`.

`GET /lens/authority/policy`	The policy in force, its source, and whether this deployment can write one.

`PUT /lens/authority/policy`	Replace it. Approver-gated, compare-and-swap on `basePolicyId`. `501` without a durable policy store.

`GET /lens/authority/policy/history`	The append-only record of every policy that has been in force.

### A reading

        Each entry carries `surfaceId` and `dimensionId`, the `state`, the `interpretation` that identifies the sink, the `contract` and its `preconditions`, the statistical `power`, any `accuracyHold` or `reSoak`, the `suspension` when there is one, and the `basis` the state was derived from. A reading is always present, so an absent surface cannot pass for a healthy one.

### The policy

        One field today, `tearAckGranularity`: `watermark` means an acknowledgement covers every tear up to it, `per-tear` means one acknowledgement per tear, applied oldest first. Unknown keys are refused rather than ignored, so a typo cannot read as a policy that silently does not apply.

        Resolution order is the operator's persisted policy, then the file seed, then the defaults. The lens never changes it: the `PUT` is the only writer and an approver gates it.

          Compare-and-swap, not last-write-wins
          The `PUT` carries the `basePolicyId` the operator reviewed. If the policy moved since, the write is refused with `authority_policy_conflict` rather than overwriting someone else's change. Reload, re-review, re-submit. The retention policy works the same way.

        The state ontology, the dependency-condition kinds, the stack and contract shapes and the pure
          state machine are public contract. Signal extraction, turning gate composition, floors, versions
          and drift into the preconditions the machine maps to a state, lives in the lens.
