### Chapter 22 — Route a verdict to a human

_Permalink: https://holonograph.ai/guide/subscriptions_

Chapter 22

# Route a verdict to a human

        The analysis chapters are **detection**: the lens reads what happened and forms a verdict. This chapter is the layer after it — **defense**. When a deterministic predicate over the lens's own verdicts fires, the lens POSTs an **HMAC-signed webhook** to a consumer you control: a pager, a chat channel, or an agent that picks up the work. It speaks only when something crosses a line — no "all quiet" pings.

          Where this sits
          The webhook is a *trigger*, not a conclusion. The usual path is: a predicate fires → a human is alerted → the human asks a coding agent to act → and the agent, before it changes anything, **consults the reliability and drift reads** (see [Verdict reliability](./sdk-reference) and [Drift attribution](./drift-attribution)) to decide whether the alert reflects real, trustworthy movement. The alert says *what* crossed a line; the reads say whether it is safe to act on.

## The shape of it

        You register a **subscription**: a predicate to watch, a window, and a webhook to call. On a schedule you own (Cloud Scheduler is the intended trigger), the lens evaluates every subscription against recent verdicts, fires the ones whose predicate matched, and **dedupes** a repeat of the same finding inside the window. The webhook secret proves the call came from your lens and nobody else.

## Create a subscription

        Writes are approver-gated. The webhook `url` must be `https`, and the `secret` is 16–512 characters. The body is strict — an unknown field is rejected.

```
POST /lens/subscriptions
Authorization: Bearer
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "predicate": { "kind": "conformance-fail", "surfaceId": "support.triage" },
  "windowMs": 300000,
  "webhook": {
    "url": "https://alerts.example.com/holonograph",
    "secret": ""
  },
  "approverId": "brian"
}
```

        Success returns `201` with a **redacted** view of the subscription: `id`, `agentId`, the predicate and window, `createdAt`/`createdBy`, and `webhook: { url }` — **the secret is write-only and is never read back**. Set it once at create; if you lose it, delete and recreate.

## Predicates — what fires an alert

        A predicate is a discriminated union on `kind`. Each names a *meaning*, never an opaque number. Three ship today:

kind	Shape	Fires when

`conformance-fail`	`{ surfaceId, fixtureId? }`	A conformance fixture FAILs on the surface (e.g. a required tool was never called). Omit `fixtureId` to fire on any fixture failure.

`emission-breach`	`{ surfaceId, columnId? }`	A substrate column declared *always-emitted* went silent in the window — a deployment is broken, not just underperforming.

`dimension-below`	`{ surfaceId, dimensionId, threshold }`	A judge dimension scored strictly below `threshold` in the window. The one predicate that reads a graded score.

## Read and delete

        Reads are also served under the `/holonograph` alias. Every read redacts the webhook secret.

Method & path	Returns

`GET /lens/subscriptions`	All subscriptions (optional `?surfaceId=` filter), each with `webhook: { url }` only.

`GET /lens/subscriptions/:id`	One subscription, or `404`.

`DELETE /lens/subscriptions/:id?approverId=`	Deletes it. `approverId` is a required query param. Returns `{ deleted: true, id }`.

        Every read returns the same projection:

Field	Shape	What it tells you

`id`	string	Server-minted. The handle for read and delete.

`agentId`	string	Derived from the contract at create time.

`predicate`	object	The predicate as registered.

`windowMs`	number	The dedupe window.

`webhook`	`{ url }`	URL only. The signing secret is write-only.

`createdAt`	ISO 8601	When it was registered.

`createdBy`	string	The approver identity that created it.

`disabled`	boolean (opt)	Paused: retained but never fires. Absent means enabled. No endpoint sets it on this release, so in practice a read returns it absent.

`lastFiredAt`	ISO 8601 (opt)	When it last fired. Absent until the first fire.

`lastFiredFingerprint`	string (opt)	The fingerprint of the last-fired match: the dedupe key the window is measured against. Compare it with the `fingerprint` on a webhook body to see whether an alert you received was the one that reset the window.

          There is no update
          Subscriptions are create / read / delete. To change a predicate, window, or webhook, **delete and recreate**. There is no edit or pause endpoint on this release.

## The webhook a consumer receives

        When a subscription fires, the lens POSTs this body to your `url`:

```
POST https://alerts.example.com/holonograph
x-holonograph-signature: sha256=
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "subscriptionId": "sub_01H...",
  "agentId": "rupert-swarm",
  "predicate": { "kind": "conformance-fail", "surfaceId": "support.triage" },
  "verdict": { /* structured, per predicate kind — the deterministic detail */ },
  "summary": "save_report was never called on support.triage",
  "fingerprint": "conformance:support.triage:...",
  "firedAt": "2026-08-22T14:03:11Z"
}
```

        `verdict` is a structured object, not a string — it carries the per-kind detail (the failing fixture and violating event ids, the silent column ids, or the dimension, threshold, and below-threshold event ids). `summary` is the one-line human sentence. `fingerprint` is the dedupe key.

### Verify the signature — first, always

        The `x-holonograph-signature` header is `sha256=` followed by the **HMAC-SHA256 of the raw request body**, keyed by the subscription's secret. Verify it over the *raw bytes you received* — before parsing JSON — and reject anything that does not match. This is the whole reason the secret exists.

```
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";

function verifyHolonographWebhook(rawBody, signatureHeader, secret) {
  const expected = "sha256=" + createHmac("sha256", secret).update(rawBody).digest("hex");
  const got = Buffer.from(signatureHeader ?? "");
  const want = Buffer.from(expected);
  // constant-time compare; length-guard first so timingSafeEqual never throws
  return got.length === want.length && timingSafeEqual(got, want);
}
```

## Required setup: the allow-list

        Delivery is **deny-by-default**. A webhook fires only to a host on the operator's allow-list; with no allow-list, **nothing fires**. Point the lens at the file with `APERTURE_WEBHOOK_ALLOWLIST_PATH` — keep it alongside your judge rubrics. It is a JSON array of hostnames:

```
// $APERTURE_WEBHOOK_ALLOWLIST_PATH
[
  "alerts.example.com",
  "localhost"
]
```

Rule	Behavior

Deny-by-default	No allow-list (absent, empty, or malformed) ⇒ every host is denied and nothing fires.

Exact hostname	Case-insensitive exact match. **No wildcards or suffixes** — `*.example.com` is not a thing; list each host.

https required	`https` for every remote host. `http` is tolerated only for loopback (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`) for local development.

No internal targets	At fire time the lens pins the resolved address and refuses private, loopback, link-local (incl. the cloud metadata address), and CGNAT ranges. It does not follow redirects.

        A demo or local bundle ships an allow-list with `localhost` in it so webhooks fire against a dev consumer.

## Firing: the evaluate cycle

        Nothing fires on its own. Point **Cloud Scheduler** (bearer-gated) at the evaluate endpoint on the cadence you want; each call is one evaluation cycle across all subscriptions.

```
POST /lens/subscriptions/evaluate
Authorization: Bearer
```

        The response is **counts only** — the silence discipline again; there is no per-subscription "all quiet":

```
{
  "evaluated": 12,
  "matched": 3,
  "fired": 2,
  "deduped": 1,
  "blocked": 0,
  "skipped": 0,
  "capped": 0,
  "allowlistConfigured": true,
  "errors": []
}
```

        A match whose `fingerprint` already fired within its `windowMs` is suppressed (`deduped`), so one broken deployment is one alert, not a storm. Dedupe state is stamped only on a *successful* delivery, so a blocked or failed send re-attempts next cycle. Each cycle fires at most 100 webhooks; matches past that are `capped` and re-attempted next cycle.

## Reference

### Endpoints

Method & path	Purpose

`POST /lens/subscriptions`	Create a subscription (approver-gated).

`GET /lens/subscriptions` · `GET /holonograph/subscriptions`	List (secret redacted). Optional `?surfaceId=`.

`GET /lens/subscriptions/:id` · `GET /holonograph/subscriptions/:id`	Read one (secret redacted).

`DELETE /lens/subscriptions/:id?approverId=`	Delete (approver-gated).

`POST /lens/subscriptions/evaluate`	Run one evaluation cycle (Cloud Scheduler; bearer-gated).

### Types

        The wire types live in `@holonograph/types-public` — `CreateSubscriptionRequest`, `SubscriptionView`, `SubscriptionPredicate`, `SubscriptionWebhookPayload`, and `EvaluateSubscriptionsResponse`. There is no subscriptions helper in `@holonograph/client`; build the requests against the types and call the endpoints over HTTP.

          Honest-null when unwired
          On a pure-collector lens with no subscription store configured, every route above answers `501` rather than pretending. The Defense layer is present only where an operator has wired it.

### Chapter 23 — Compaction & husking

_Permalink: https://holonograph.ai/guide/compaction_

Chapter 23

# Compaction & husking

        Compaction removes the bulky payload from an aging event and keeps every structured field any estimator reads. The lens never compacts on its own.

## What it is

        An operator-invoked pipeline: plan, verify, seal, move. Three endpoints, and the first of them
          writes nothing.

Endpoint	Behavior

`POST /lens/retention/plan`	Always a dry run. Reports what would be compacted and writes nothing.

`POST /lens/retention/compact`	Executes an approved plan. Approver-gated.

`POST /lens/retention/unseal`	Undoes an archive-mode seal.

### Retention classes

        Every event kind declares one. The enumeration is exhaustive, so a new event kind fails the type
          check until it has been classified.

Class	Meaning

`never`	Never compacted. Evidence, markers and seals.

`husk`	Payload may be archived or deleted; structured fields are kept.

`summarise`	Compactable only into lossless summaries.

## Why it matters

### A husk is a projection, not a new fact

        Husking keeps every structured field an estimator reads: ids, `occurredAt`, the whole
          substrate, the surface grading including dimension scores, judge identity and structured claims,
          gate outcomes, cohort tags, light identity and accounting. What leaves is bulk:
          `light.rawRequest`, `rawResponse`, `reasoning`,
          `toolCalls`, `vendorMetadata`, `error.message`, each dimension's
          `rationale`, `sideEffects[].details`, and oversized unknown keys.

        Where the payload went is recorded on the husk. `archived` means a sealed,
          hash-chained archive segment holds the full event and the operator can unseal it.
          `deleted` means it is gone and only the digest remains. `erased` means a
          right-to-delete request removed it.

### The stamp cannot be forged

        A husk stamp is server-projected. It exists only on husks the compactor wrote into a sealed husk
          segment, it is never written onto a stored raw event, and every producer ingest path rejects an
          event that arrives carrying one. A forged stamp would claim facts the lens never extracted.

### Payload-reading consumers keep working

        Some consumers read the payload: verdict reliability, co-groundedness, trajectory, exemplars. The
          husk carries a `facts` block holding those extractors' outputs, computed over the raw
          event at seal time and stamped with each extractor's version. A consumer whose extractor version
          or configuration no longer matches reports a method boundary rather than a clean result.

## How to use it

          - Plan first and read the plan. It is a dry run by construction, not by flag.

          - Compact against an approved plan. The approval is the gate.

          - Prefer archive mode where the payload may be wanted again; an archive seal can be unsealed, a delete cannot.

          - Every consumer of event history declares its post-compaction fidelity, so check that declaration before compacting a span an analysis still depends on.

## Reading the output

        A compacted span reads the same as an uncompacted one for every structured consumer. Scores,
          grading, gate outcomes and identity are unchanged, because none of them lived in the payload. A
          reading that cannot be reproduced on a husk says so as a method boundary.

## The retention policy

        A policy is a standing disposition the operator approved. The lens never adopts one: the `store-capacity` finding recommends a preset and stops there. Under `schedule: manual` nothing runs on its own; under `schedule: auto` each nightly run remains that same approved disposition, and each one mints a seal and a spine entry.

Method & path	Purpose

`GET /lens/retention/policy`	The policy in force, its `source` (`operator`, `file` or `default`), the operator record, whether `PUT` is available here, and whether a file seed is being ignored.

`PUT /lens/retention/policy`	Replace it. Approver-gated, compare-and-swap on `basePolicyId`, and a delete-mode policy needs an explicit acknowledgement. Appends to the durable history, then mints the audit record. `501` without a policy store.

`GET /lens/retention/policy/history`	Every operator policy, oldest first.

`GET /lens/retention/schedule`	The schedule and the auto-run log. Reports `supported: false` where it cannot run.

`GET /lens/retention/compaction`	Status: tiers, seals, chain head, any interrupted operation. `?verify=true` re-reads every segment and checks the chain.

`POST /lens/retention/compaction/prepare`	The one-time index preparation a backend needs before its first compaction. Approver-gated and explicit; the filesystem backend needs none.

          A read-window override naming an undeclared surface is a warning
          The policy schema refuses duplicate or ambiguous read-window overrides and unknown run modes outright. An override naming a surface the contract does not declare is accepted instead, with a `warnings` entry: the contract may be about to declare it, and refusing would make policy and contract impossible to deploy in either order.

## Archive, rehydrate and erasure

        Sealed segments can be mounted back for reading, and data can be removed on request. Every write here is approver-gated, because the lens rehydrates and erases on no one's initiative but the operator's.

Method & path	Purpose

`GET /lens/archive/overlays`	The mounted rehydrate overlays. Also reported on health.

`POST /lens/archive/rehydrate`	Mount archive segments as a read-only overlay with a TTL, selected by `segmentIds`, `window` or `decompositionEventId`. Verifies the chain and footer digests and decrypts where needed. Nothing is appended.

`POST /lens/archive/unmount`	End an overlay before its TTL.

`POST /lens/archive/erase/plan`	A dry run of a right-to-delete erasure: the members by tier, the seals it re-segments, the segments it shreds, the frozen windows it touches, what is removed and what survives. Writes nothing.

`POST /lens/archive/erase`	Execute a reviewed plan. Approver-gated and requires `acknowledgeIrreversible: true`; the server re-plans and refuses a plan that has moved.

        An overlay is read-only and expires. Rehydrating does not reverse a compaction: it makes a sealed span readable for as long as the TTL lasts, and appends nothing. A backend without the archive surface answers the read with `{ supported: false, reason }` and every write with `501`, rather than an empty success.

## Reference

          - On Firestore, compaction is opt-in and never edits a record in order to build its index.

          - The judge-verdict linking model is husk-invariant: a husked event resolves the same verdict a whole one does.

          - Retention policy and schedule are stored durably and are operator-owned.
